CARVEYANCE How It Works

How It Works · The Cleverest Gearbox Nobody Remembers

The Little Dutch Car That Went Backward As Fast As It Went Forward

It had two rubber belts, no gears, and a control system made of springs and suction. It embarrassed real rally cars, spawned a national sport of racing in reverse, and got itself banned from Formula One. Christopher Nolan needed a nine-figure budget to sell you that idea. DAF was selling it to Dutch pensioners in 1959.

By Oliver Bacon · How It Works · DAF & the Variomatic · 17 min read

Civic. Kayak. Rotator. Racecar — which, in a car magazine, feels like the universe showing its work. These are palindromes: words that read identically in either direction, and the most famous recent one is Tenet, Christopher Nolan's film about time running forward and backward at the same moment.

I should come clean here. I saw Tenet. I could not follow it in either direction. I am not entirely convinced it was not following me. Somewhere in the second half I became certain I had already seen the film, just from the other end, which I am reliably informed is either the entire point or a sign that I should have eaten beforehand.

What survives the confusion is the shape of the thing. The essence is symmetry — forward and backward, same speed, at once, and it scarcely matters which way you run it. Nolan needed a nine-figure budget, an inverted-time conceit and Robert Pattinson to make that idea legible on a screen.

A small Dutch company had already built it into a shopping car. In 1959. For pensioners. And then an entire country turned it into a televised sport.

Growing up in Hong Kong meant becoming accustomed to automotive surprises. It was the kind of place where an unfamiliar badge could pass by and leave you wondering whether you had discovered a new manufacturer or simply hallucinated in the humidity. The traffic offered an improbable mixture of Japanese-market oddities, European commercial vehicles, British leftovers and serious exotics, and every so often a Ferrari 288 GTO would appear — an especially baffling choice in a city where traffic, geography and speed limits made exploiting one about as practical as keeping a thoroughbred racehorse in a studio apartment. You could admire it. You could polish it. You could move twelve feet before encountering another taxi.

Hong Kong's emergency fleet added to the confusion. I remember large European machines, some wearing MAN badges and others carrying three unfamiliar letters, the whole collection of imported chassis and specialist bodywork looking like a rolling catalog of European heavy industry. One day, riding with my father, I read the letters aloud. DAF.

My father told me that DAF had once made cars — and not ordinary ones. They were belt-driven, he said, with a simple forward-and-reverse selector that worked more like the control on a boat than a gear lever, and because the transmission offered the same range of ratios in either direction, the car could go backward almost as fast as it could go forward.

I was in roughly the fourth grade, and that was all I needed to hear. A belt-driven car that could reach maximum velocity in reverse? Forget horsepower. Forget top speed. Forget the Lamborghini poster. This was clearly the work of either a genius or a lunatic, and preferably both.

As it turns out, my father was essentially correct. He was also only telling me the first ten percent of it.

A Small Country With a Long Habit of Solving Awkward Problems

The Dutch invented a great deal more than you think

The Netherlands has contributed a wildly disproportionate amount to the modern world. This is a country that learned to take land back from the sea, manage water with a sophistication bordering on the theological, and build a global trading empire from a landscape that occasionally needs reminding not to become part of the North Sea.

The list runs long and strange. Dutch hands shaped maritime trade and shipbuilding, cartography and navigation, hydraulic engineering and flood control. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek put a lens to a drop of pond water and found an entire kingdom nobody had known was there. Christiaan Huygens worked out the pendulum clock and much of what we understand about timekeeping. Amsterdam gave the world the first modern stock exchange, which has been variously a blessing and a bill. Later came Philips, the compact cassette, a share of the compact disc, and — this one delights me — Bluetooth, developed under the technical leadership of the Dutch engineer Jaap Haartsen, which is why the thing in your ear is named after a tenth century Danish king by way of an office park outside Eindhoven.

The automotive contribution is less celebrated but far from trivial. Spyker built an extraordinary machine in 1903 that combined a six-cylinder engine, four-wheel drive and four-wheel braking at a moment when most cars were still deciding whether brakes were a good idea at all. Donkervoort has spent decades building featherweight sports cars for people with strong necks. Dutch engineering firms became quietly essential in automotive electronics, lighting, navigation and transmission development.

But the most wonderfully Dutch contribution of all may be DAF's Variomatic, which solved a genuinely difficult problem using pulleys, vacuum, centrifugal force and a pair of large rubber belts. It was ingenious, practical, slightly peculiar, and enormously more influential than its humble appearance ever suggested.

Eindhoven, 1928

From trailers to tiny cars

DAF began with two brothers, Hub and Wim van Doorne. Hub opened a small engineering workshop in Eindhoven in 1928, the company moved into trailers, and it took the name Van Doorne's Aanhangwagen Fabriek — Van Doorne's Trailer Factory. When the ambition outgrew trailers the name became Van Doorne's Automobiel Fabriek. Conveniently, both abbreviate to DAF, which saved a fortune in signage.

The company became a serious producer of trucks, commercial vehicles and military machinery, and DAF trucks are still built today under PACCAR ownership. Passenger cars, however, were a different adventure entirely. Post-war Europe needed cheap personal transportation, and Hub van Doorne wanted to build something economical, approachable and exceptionally easy to drive. He reportedly disliked the whole business of changing gears, and did not believe an ordinary person should have to master a clutch and a gate full of ratios simply to reach the shops.

His answer was the Variomatic. And to understand why it matters, you have to understand what it actually did — which is easier to watch than to read.

The Idea

A transmission with no gears, at least not in the usual sense

A conventional manual gearbox offers a handful of fixed ratios. First gear gives strong acceleration at low speed, and each subsequent gear trades torque multiplication for road speed. The Variomatic did not step from one fixed ratio to another. It simply changed, all the time, by tiny amounts, forever.

The hardware was almost insultingly simple: two variable-diameter pulleys with conical faces, a V-shaped drive belt, some centrifugal weights, springs, vacuum diaphragms, a supply of engine manifold vacuum, and a few mechanical linkages. Each pulley was a pair of cones facing one another. Move them closer and the belt rode outward toward the rim, making the pulley effectively larger. Move them apart and the belt fell inward toward the shaft, making it smaller. When the driving pulley grew while the driven pulley shrank, the ratio went taller; reverse the relationship and it went lower for acceleration or climbing.

Where a manual gearbox says first, second, third, fourth, the DAF said: a little lower, a little higher, a little higher still, whatever this precise moment requires. There was no perceptible shift because there were no steps to shift between.

We call this a continuously variable transmission now, or CVT, and we mostly associate it with sensible commuting appliances. In the late 1950s, when automatic transmissions were large, thirsty, expensive hydraulic contraptions generally reserved for big cars, DAF was fitting a compact mechanical version to a tiny Dutch economy car. A British firm, Clyno, had experimented with the idea as far back as 1923, so DAF cannot claim the very first. What DAF can claim is vastly more important: it built the first one anybody could actually go out and buy in numbers.

Every other engineer in Europe was arguing about how many gears a small car needed. Hub van Doorne's answer was to ask why it needed any.

No Transistors Were Harmed

A mechanical computer made of suction and spinning weights

A modern CVT is governed by an electronic control unit reading speed, throttle position, engine load, temperature, braking and a dozen other inputs several hundred times a second. DAF achieved much the same decision-making without a single transistor.

Centrifugal weights responded to rotational speed — the faster the shaft spun, the harder they were flung outward, and the harder they pushed the cone faces together. Engine vacuum did the other half of the job. Manifold vacuum is high when the throttle is barely open and collapses when you plant your foot, which makes it a beautifully direct analog of how much the driver is asking for. Springs and diaphragms converted those two signals into physical cone movement.

So at light throttle, with strong vacuum, the transmission drifted toward a tall, economical ratio. Bury the accelerator, the vacuum signal collapsed, and the Variomatic promptly slid back down to a lower ratio for acceleration. It did not think in any electronic sense. It simply interpreted, continuously and mechanically, what the engine and the driver were doing. Speed, load, vacuum and spring pressure were its programming language — and it ran that program while looking like farm machinery hiding beneath a family car.

The Part That Should Not Work

Two belts, two rear wheels, and no differential at all

The early Variomatic DAFs were stranger still. Almost every car needs a differential, because the outside wheel travels farther than the inside wheel through a corner; lock them rigidly together and one of them has to slip, scrub and complain. DAF's solution was to give each rear wheel its own belt and its own variable-pulley set. Because the left and right pulley pairs could settle at slightly different ratios, the two rear wheels could turn at different speeds without anyone having to build a differential at all.

The transmission therefore held down two jobs at once. It varied the drive ratio, and it performed the differential action required for cornering. Better still, the arrangement produced something close to a limited-slip effect, because one spinning wheel did not automatically swallow all the useful drive the way a simple open differential allows. This is the reason a tiny automatic Dutch economy car turned out to be startlingly good on snow, mud, wet roads and loose rally surfaces — places where absolutely nobody expected to find one.

It was not free of drawbacks. The belts had to be correctly adjusted and reasonably well matched to one another. Vacuum lines, diaphragms, pulleys and belts all wanted maintenance, and oil contamination, age, corrosion or careless adjustment could turn clever engineering into baffling behavior remarkably quickly. But when it was right, it was delightful.

The Famous Bit

And yes, it really would go that fast backward

My father's story was not folklore. A normal gearbox gives you several forward ratios and precisely one low reverse, which is why reversing quickly feels like an act of aggression against the machinery. The DAF's entire continuously variable range remained available after the direction of travel was reversed — the Variomatic simply ran backward through the same set of ratios. Mechanically, that meant a DAF could reach very nearly the same speed in reverse as it could going forward.

This did not make high-speed reversing remotely sensible. The car still had steering geometry designed for forward stability, seats facing the wrong way for the occasion, limited rearward visibility, aerodynamics developed on the assumption that the front would go first, and a driver equipped with only one neck. Naturally, people raced them backward.

What began as a novelty became a genuine Dutch institution. Reverse racing — achteruitrijden — found a home on television through the long-running TROS program Te land, ter zee en in de lucht, with events at Zandvoort and the Eurocircuit at Valkenswaard and the comedian André van Duin narrating the carnage. Cars charged backward around circuits, steering with the back end, navigating by mirror and over-the-shoulder guesswork, exchanging body panels and dignity in roughly equal measure. The DAFs were so completely dominant that organizers eventually gave them a category of their own, partly for fairness and partly for everyone's safety.

The tradition never quite died. In 2025, ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix, Red Bull revived it at Zandvoort and put Max Verstappen and Yuki Tsunoda in a pair of DAF 66s fitted with roll cages and four-point harnesses, to race each other backward around a Formula One circuit. A reigning world champion, going the wrong way, in a Dutch shopping car built before he was born. Verstappen won.

Unfortunately the joke tended to eclipse the engineering. The Variomatic was a great deal more than a party trick for people who considered mirrors optional. It was a serious attempt to rethink how a car should transmit power — and the joke cost DAF dearly, because a company known for a car that goes backward comically fast is not a company known for a car that goes forward intelligently well.

1958

The DAF 600: small car, enormous idea

DAF showed its first production passenger car at the Amsterdam motor show in February 1958, and the response was immediate — around four thousand orders were placed for a car that was not yet entirely ready to be built. Production began in 1959. It was a compact two-door with a 590 cc air-cooled flat-twin making 22 horsepower, rear-wheel drive, independent suspension, no clutch pedal, and the Variomatic. At just over twelve feet long it turned in a tighter circle than a Volkswagen Beetle, and it was not fast in either direction, which was entirely beside the point.

The 600 offered inexpensive transportation almost anyone could operate. You chose a direction, pressed the accelerator, and let the transmission work out the rest. The Dutch nicknamed the mechanism het pientere pookje — roughly, the clever little lever. The advertising was equally direct: forwards to go forwards, back to go back. When DAF later tried the United States, it went with a line that deserves preserving in amber — shift to DAF, you'll never shift again.

There is a lovely footnote to the launch. The first two cars off the line were presented to the chairman of the Dutch automobile club and to Truus Smulders-Beliën, the first woman in the Netherlands to serve as a mayor. She had reportedly been chosen because she was well known and because records showed she had ordered one. It emerged that her staff had ordered it. She had not, and she did not hold a driving license. She accepted the car anyway, which is the most Dutch resolution available.

DAF 600 — 1959

A family followed: the 750 and the cheerfully named Daffodil, then the 33, the 44, the 55, the 66 and finally the 46. The names lack the resonance of 911, Mustang or Testarossa. The engineering underneath them was considerably more unconventional than any of the three.

How many Dutchmen bought the idea

Production totals for the main Variomatic models. The 55 — the one that went rallying — is also the one that sold hardest.

DAF 55164,231
DAF Daffodil132,919
DAF 60030,591
DAF 75016,767

Modest numbers by Wolfsburg standards, and beside the point. DAF was not trying to out-produce the Beetle. It was proving that a continuously variable transmission could be built, sold, serviced and survived — which nobody had yet managed.

Michelotti Gets Involved

From cheerful economy car to Italian tailoring

The earliest DAFs were practical and friendly-looking in the way a garden shed is friendly- looking. The later ones grew up. The DAF 44, introduced in the mid-1960s, was styled by Giovanni Michelotti, the enormously prolific Italian designer behind numerous Triumphs, BMWs and Alpines. Yes — even the tiny belt-driven Dutch car got Italian tailoring. It kept the air-cooled flat-twin, but it was larger, more polished and far more convincingly car-shaped than the 600.

Then came the DAF 55, which threw out the little flat-twin in favor of a water-cooled 1,108 cc Renault four, and arrived as a saloon, an estate and a genuinely handsome coupe. The extra power revealed something important: the Variomatic did not have to live its whole life inside very slow economy cars. It also handed DAF something to go rallying with.

The Image Problem, and the Cure

The automatic little car that went rallying anyway

DAF knew exactly what its reputation was. Because the cars were small and effortless to operate, they had become associated with elderly and timid drivers — people who either could not or would not shift for themselves. This was unfair, but image rarely waits around for the engineering evidence to come in.

DAF's response was the correct one: take the supposedly delicate automatic rallying and find out what breaks. The cars were entered in the Monte Carlo, the Alpine, the Acropolis, the Tulip, and a long list of national and European events. A DAF 55 won the 1968 Alpine Rally outright.

And then there was the Marathon. The 1968 London–Sydney Marathon ran 10,373 miles (16,694 km) across Europe, the Middle East, Asia and Australia, from Crystal Palace to Sydney, with a boat in the middle and very little mercy at either end. Ninety-eight crews started. Fifty-six finished. Rob Slotemaker brought his DAF 55 home seventeenth overall — in a 1.1-liter automatic that had the smallest engine in the entire field, against works teams running Hillmans, Fords, Citroëns and Austins with two and three times the displacement. A second DAF also reached Sydney. The company was so pleased that it named a whole performance package Marathon and sold it through the dealers.

A 1.1-liter Dutch automatic crossed eleven countries and two continents, and beat four out of every five cars that started.

The competition advantage was real, and it is worth understanding because it explains everything that happens next. A driver with a manual gearbox accelerates through the power band, changes gear, falls out of the useful rev range, and climbs back into it. A properly calibrated Variomatic could take the engine to the exact speed where it made its best power and simply leave it there, varying the ratio underneath instead. The engine no longer had to chase the gearbox. The gearbox followed the engine.

Then It Got Out of Hand

Jan de Rooy builds a monster

If crossing Asia was insufficient proof, the Dutch driver Jan de Rooy — later famous for Dakar — set about building DAF-based rallycross machines through the early 1970s. These were emphatically not standard DAFs with stripes down the side. They combined mid-mounted Ford BDA engines, specially built Variomatic units, four-wheel drive, lightweight bodywork, vastly more power than any road-going DAF had ever seen, and roughly the temperament of an industrial accident. They were savagely quick, and they demonstrated that belt-driven variable transmissions could handle serious competition when they were engineered for it.

The same idea appeared in single-seat Formula 3 machinery. And then, two decades later, it turned up somewhere nobody was ready for it.

1993

From a tiny DAF to a Williams Formula One car

DAF's transmission business evolved into Van Doorne's Transmissie, and it moved on from rubber to develop the steel push-belt CVT, which could handle far more torque than anything the 600 ever dreamed of. In 1993, Williams — then comprehensively the best team in Formula One — fitted one to an FW15C.

The principle was exactly the one that made the little DAF so strange. Rather than stepping through fixed gears, the transmission could hold the Renault V10 at the engine speed where it made its 780 horsepower and keep it there while the ratio changed continuously underneath. David Coulthard tested the car at a wet Pembrey in Wales; the touring car driver Alain Menu drove it too. To a spectator it sounded genuinely wrong — instead of rising and falling through each corner, the engine simply arrived at an ear-splitting note and stayed there while the car kept accelerating.

Reports of the gain vary from around a second a lap to several. What is not in dispute is what happened next. The 1994 regulations required every car to have between four and seven fixed gears, and then, to remove any possible ambiguity about how many gears a CVT has — one? none? all of them? — the FIA added a sub-clause naming continuously variable transmissions specifically and banning them. The Williams CVT never raced. A technology associated with economy cars, cautious drivers and comedy reverse racing had become threatening enough that the rulebook was rewritten to keep it out.

One small correction to a story often repeated, including in the version I grew up with: the car spent years on display at the DAF Museum in Eindhoven, which is a wonderfully fitting place for it, but Williams eventually asked for it back and it returned to England.

1975

Volvo buys the cars, and the idea escapes

By the 1970s DAF's passenger-car operation needed investment the company could not comfortably find, and Volvo wanted something smaller to sit beneath its sensible sedans and estates. Volvo acquired the car division progressively and took control in 1975. The DAF 66 became the Volvo 66, gaining Volvo badges and a set of safety revisions while keeping the Variomatic. A larger car DAF had been developing became the Volvo 343; early ones still used the Variomatic, manual gearboxes arrived later, and the design grew into the long-lived Volvo 340 and 360 family. Which means a boxy Volvo hatchback of the 1980s carries a good deal more Dutch DNA than its badge lets on.

The DAF passenger-car name disappeared. The transmission work did not. Van Doorne's steel push-belt technology spread through the industry and made the modern CVT viable in larger, more powerful, higher-volume applications, and today continuously variable transmissions turn up in millions of vehicles from Toyota, Honda, Nissan, Subaru, Mitsubishi and most of the hybrid world.

An honest caveat belongs here, because the internet tends to overclaim it. Not every modern CVT is a direct mechanical descendant of the Variomatic, and the hybrid e-CVT in a Prius is not a belt-and-pulley device at all — it uses a planetary power-split arrangement that works on entirely different principles. What is fair to say is that DAF was among the handful of companies that proved a continuously variable transmission could be manufactured, sold, raced, serviced and improved, and that the Dutch firm which grew out of it supplied a great deal of the technology that made the modern version work.

The Verdict

Considerably more important than it looks

A DAF is very easy to underestimate. It has none of the beauty of a 288 GTO, none of the theater of a Lamborghini, none of the competition mythology of an Integrale. Most of them are small cheerful things with engines that would struggle to intimidate a riding mower.

And yet underneath that modest body sits a genuinely radical proposition, one that delivered a practical mass-produced CVT, automatic ratio selection for cars too cheap to justify a conventional automatic, load-sensitive control achieved without a single electronic component, independent twin-belt drive, differential action as a by-product of the gearbox, limited-slip traction nobody asked for, constant-rpm performance running, and a development path that leads directly to the transmission in a great many driveways today. That is a substantial legacy for a company whose cars most enthusiasts have never heard of.

Which brings me back to Hong Kong, sitting in the car with my father, sounding out three unfamiliar letters on the front of a European truck. At the time it was simply another strange badge in a city full of automotive contradictions, a place where a 288 GTO could sit in traffic and every parking garage held something worth a second look. But my father gave that badge a story: a little Dutch car driven by belts, controlled rather like a boat, capable of going backward nearly as fast as it went forward.

It sounded impossible, ridiculous and brilliant. More than anything, it sounded Dutch.
